chapters.title: Chapter 3: Central Bank Coordination and Divergence

lessons.title: The RBI's Place in the Global Liquidity Cycle: MPC, Reserves, and Policy Autonomy

body.text: The RBI has real autonomy, but it is bounded autonomy. Its Monetary Policy Committee sets policy for a purely domestic inflation target, yet India's exchange rate arrangement and partially open capital account mean the global liquidity cycle still shapes how much room that autonomy actually has.

children.text: Since the RBI Act was amended in 2016, India has run a formal inflation-targeting framework. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), six members in total, the RBI Governor as chair, the RBI Deputy Governor overseeing monetary policy, one RBI-nominated officer, and three external members appointed by the central government, sets the repo rate by majority vote, with the Governor holding a casting vote in the event of a tie. Its legal mandate is to keep CPI inflation at 4%, within a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. Nowhere in that mandate does the exchange rate or FPI flows appear explicitly. And yet, as this lesson shows, they are never far from the room.
The Impossible Trinity: Why No Country Gets Everything

A well-established idea in international macroeconomics, often called the impossible trinity or the trilemma, holds that no country can simultaneously have all three of: free cross-border capital flow, a fixed or tightly managed exchange rate, and fully independent monetary policy. A country can pick any two, but the third has to give.

body.caption: The Impossible Trinity: Pick Two, Give Up the Third

cells: Free capital flow + fixed exchange rate
Independent monetary policy (rates must track the anchor currency)
Capital mobility and your own rate decisions
A stable, fixed exchange rate (the US and most developed markets sit here)
Currency stability and your own rate decisions
Free capital flow (requires capital controls, closer to China's model)

children.text: India does not sit cleanly in any single corner of this triangle. It runs a managed float, not a fixed rate, and a partially open capital account, not a fully open or fully closed one. That middle path is deliberate: it buys India a meaningful, though not unlimited, degree of monetary independence, at the cost of occasional, visible RBI intervention in the currency market to keep the rupee from moving too sharply in either direction.

body.title: Where India Sits Between the Two Extremes

columns.label: PBOC / China
points: Tight capital controls, currency managed close to a target band
High degree of monetary policy independence from the Fed as a result
Trade-off: capital cannot move freely in or out of the renminbi

columns.label: RBI / India
points: Partially open capital account, managed float rather than a fixed rate
Meaningful but bounded monetary independence, cushioned by active FX intervention
Trade-off: reserves must be deployed periodically to smooth rupee volatility

columns.label: Fed / United States
points: Fully open capital account, freely floating dollar
Full monetary policy independence, sets policy purely for domestic goals
Trade-off: none from its own perspective, the dollar's reserve status means the rest of the world absorbs the spillover

children.text: Forex Reserves: The Tool That Makes the Middle Path Work

Forex reserves are what let the RBI run a managed float instead of being forced into a clean corner of the trilemma. By buying dollars when inflows are strong and selling them when outflows pressure the rupee, the RBI smooths currency volatility without fully fixing the exchange rate and without fully giving up its own policy rate decisions. This is exactly the tool that was thin in 2013 and comparatively strong in 2022, as covered in the previous chapter.

body.label: India's Forex Reserves, Recent Years
body.context: India's reserves have grown into one of the larger stockpiles among emerging markets, giving the RBI substantial room to intervene. Check the RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement for the current figure, since it moves week to week with both valuation changes and intervention.

body.text: The MPC's mandate is domestic CPI inflation, not the exchange rate. But a weakening rupee raises the price of imported oil, edible oils and other dollar-priced goods, which shows up directly in the CPI basket the MPC is legally targeting. This is why the RBI ends up watching global liquidity conditions closely even though its formal mandate never mentions the dollar, the Fed or FPI flows: the exchange rate is a transmission channel into the inflation number it is actually responsible for.

body.title: Inflation Is Fine, the Rupee Is Not
body.scenario: Domestic CPI inflation is comfortably within the RBI's 2% to 6% target band. At the same time, the Fed is hiking aggressively, the dollar is strengthening broadly, and the rupee is depreciating faster than the RBI is comfortable with.
body.prompt: Strictly by its legal mandate, the MPC has no obligation to react to rupee weakness on its own. Why might the RBI still act, and what tools could it use that do not require the MPC to change the repo rate at all?
body.modelAnswer: Even though the MPC's formal mandate is CPI inflation, not the exchange rate, a rapidly weakening rupee threatens to raise imported inflation later, which would eventually show up in the very CPI number the MPC targets. So there is a legitimate, mandate-consistent reason to act preemptively. Critically, the RBI does not need to change the repo rate to respond. It can sell dollars from its forex reserves directly in the currency market to slow the rupee's fall, it can use forward market intervention, or it can lean on tools like NRI deposit schemes similar to the 2013 FCNR(B) swap. These tools let the RBI manage currency pressure from the global liquidity cycle without necessarily forcing the MPC's hand on the policy rate itself.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: According to the impossible trinity, what does a country give up if it chooses free capital flow and a fixed exchange rate?
options: Independent monetary policy, since rates must track the anchor currency
body.explanation: Under the impossible trinity, a country can only hold two of the three: free capital flow, a fixed exchange rate, and independent monetary policy. Choosing free capital flow plus a fixed exchange rate means domestic interest rates must effectively track the anchor currency's rates, since any gap would trigger capital flows large enough to break the fixed rate.

points: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee has a legally domestic mandate: CPI inflation at 4%, within a 2% to 6% band, decided by majority vote among six members.

The impossible trinity means no country can have free capital flow, a fixed exchange rate, and independent monetary policy all at once; India's managed float and partial capital controls are a deliberate middle path.
Forex reserves are the tool that makes India's middle path workable, letting the RBI smooth currency volatility without fully fixing the rupee or fully surrendering rate independence.
The exchange rate is not in the MPC's formal mandate, but it feeds into CPI inflation through imported goods, which is why the RBI still watches the global liquidity cycle closely.
The RBI has tools, like FX intervention and NRI deposit schemes, that let it manage currency pressure from global liquidity without necessarily changing the repo rate itself.
